claim: Spatial attention changes the sampling of visual space.
source: Spatial attention changes the sampling of visual space.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general principle supported by the study's findings.

claim: Behavioral studies suggest that feature-based attention modulates resampling to optimize the attended feature's sampling.
source: Behavioral studies suggest that feature-based attention modulates this resampling to optimize the attended feature's sampling.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to behavioral studies mentioned in the introduction.

claim: Spatial and feature-based attention interacted such that resampling of visual space depended on both the attended location and feature (color vs. temporal frequency).
source: Our results show that spatial and feature-based attention interacted: resampling of visual space depended on both the attended location and feature (color vs. temporal frequency).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: The interaction between spatial and feature-based attention occurred similarly throughout visual cortex, regardless of an area's overall feature preference.
source: This interaction occurred similarly throughout visual cortex, regardless of an area's overall feature preference.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on analysis across multiple visual regions.

claim: The interaction between spatial and feature-based attention depended on spatial sampling properties of voxels that prefer the attended feature.
source: However, the interaction did depend on spatial sampling properties of voxels that prefer the attended feature.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on analysis of voxel properties.

claim: The findings are parsimoniously explained by variations in the precision of an attentional gain field.
source: These findings are parsimoniously explained by variations in the precision of an attentional gain field.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on modeling results presented in the study.

claim: The deployment of spatial attention is tailored to the spatial sampling properties of units that are sensitive to the attended feature.
source: Our results demonstrate that the deployment of spatial attention is tailored to the spatial sampling properties of units that are sensitive to the attended feature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The resolution of the visual system is highest at the fovea and decreases gradually with increasing eccentricity.
source: The resolution of the visual system is highest at the fovea and decreases gradually with increasing eccentricity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the visual system.

claim: Attention can be directed to a location in space and/or a visual feature, which temporarily improves behavioral performance.
source: Attention can be directed to a location in space and/or a visual feature, which temporarily improves behavioral performance (Posner et al., 1980; Rossi and Paradiso, 1995; Found and Müller, 1996; Carrasco and Yeshurun, 1998; Yeshurun and Carrasco, 1999; Kumada, 2001; Sàenz et al., 2003; Wolfe et al., 2003; Theeuwes and Van der Burg, 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Attention improves performance at the cost of reduced sensitivity for non-attended locations and features.
source: at the cost of reduced sensitivity for non-attended locations and features (Kastner and Pinsk, 2004; Pestilli and Carrasco, 2005; Wegener et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Attending a location in space increases activity in units representing the attended location, as shown by both electrophysiological and fMRI studies.
source: Attending a location in space increases activity in units representing the attended location, as shown by both electrophysiological (Luck et al., 1997; Reynolds et al., 2000) and fMRI studies (Tootell et al., 1998; Silver et al., 2005; Datta and DeYoe, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to electrophysiological and fMRI studies.

claim: Spatial receptive fields shift toward an attended location in macaque MT+ and V4.
source: In addition, spatial receptive fields were shown to shift toward an attended location in macaque MT+ (Womelsdorf et al., 2006) and V4 (Connor et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to electrophysiological studies in macaques.

claim: pRF shifts induced by spatial attention occur throughout human visual cortex.
source: Using fMRI to measure population receptive fields (pRFs; Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008; Dumoulin and Knapen, 2018), it was found that pRF shifts induced by spatial attention occur throughout human visual cortex (Klein et al., 2014; Kay et al., 2015; Sheremata and Silver, 2015; Vo et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to fMRI studies.

claim: pRF shifts are thought to improve visual resolution at the attended location.
source: a process thought to improve visual resolution at the attended location (Anton-Erxleben and Carrasco, 2013; Kay et al., 2015; Vo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Spatial resampling is understood to be the result of an interaction between bottom-up sensory signals and a top-down attentional gain field.
source: Such spatial resampling is understood to be the result of an interaction between bottom-up sensory signals and a top-down attentional gain field (Womelsdorf et al., 2008; Klein et al., 2014; Miconi and VanRullen, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to modeling studies.

claim: Feature-based attention selectively increases activity in units that represent the attended feature, as evidenced by electrophysiological, fMRI, and behavioral reports.
source: Feature-based attention, for example directed toward color or motion, selectively increases activity in those units that represent the attended feature, as evidenced by electrophysiological (Treue and Maunsell, 1996; Treue et al., 1999; McAdams and Maunsell, 2000; Maunsell and Treue, 2006; Müller et al., 2006; Zhang and Luck, 2009; Zhou and Desimone, 2011), fMRI (Saenz et al., 2002; Serences and Boynton, 2007; Jehee et al., 2011), and behavioral reports (Sàenz et al., 2003; White and Carrasco, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to different types of studies.

claim: Feature-based attention modulates processing irrespective of the attended stimulus's spatial location.
source: These studies consistently show that feature-based attention modulates processing irrespective of the attended stimulus's spatial location.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: Feature-based attention shifts featural tuning curves toward the attended value, as reported by both electrophysiological and fMRI studies.
source: In addition, feature-based attention also appears to shift featural tuning curves toward the attended value, as reported by both electrophysiological (Motter, 1994; David et al., 2008) and fMRI studies (Çukur et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to electrophysiological and fMRI studies.

claim: The similarity in the effects of feature-based and spatial attention on affected neural units suggests a common neural mechanism for both sources of attention.
source: The similarity in the effects of feature-based and spatial attention on affected neural units suggests a common neural mechanism for both sources of attention (Hayden and Gallant, 2005; Cohen and Maunsell, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Spatial attention necessitates retinotopically precise feedback.
source: Yet spatial attention necessitates retinotopically precise feedback (Miconi and VanRullen, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a modeling study.

claim: Feature-based attention operates throughout the visual field.
source: whereas feature-based attention operates throughout the visual field (Maunsell and Treue, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Interactions between spatial and feature-based attention are either nonexistent or very weak at the earliest stages of processing.
source: Studies investigating whether one source of attention potentiates the other generally find that interactions are either nonexistent or very weak at the earliest stages of processing (David et al., 2008; Hayden and Gallant, 2009; Patzwahl and Treue, 2009; Zhang and Luck, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Interactions between spatial and feature-based attention emerge at later stages of visual processing.
source: but emerge at later stages of visual processing (Hillyard and Münte, 1984; Handy et al., 2001; Bengson et al., 2012; Ibos and Freedman, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Interactions between spatial and feature-based attention ultimately influence behavior.
source: and ultimately influence behavior (Kingstone, 1992; Kravitz and Behrmann, 2011; Leonard et al., 2015; White et al., 2015; Nordfang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: The effects of feature-based compared to spatial attention arise earlier in time.
source: In addition, the effects of feature-based compared to spatial attention arise earlier in time. This occurs both when only feature-based attention is endogenously cued and subsequently guides spatial attention towards the attended feature's location (Hopf et al., 2004), and when both types of attention are endogenously cued (Hayden and Gallant, 2005; Andersen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Feature-based attention can direct spatial attention toward or away from specific locations containing attended or unattended features.
source: This supports the idea that feature-based attention can direct spatial attention toward or away from specific locations containing attended or unattended features (Cohen and Shoup, 1997; Cepeda et al., 1998; Burnett et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: No study to date has investigated the effect of feature-based attention on spatial sampling.
source: However, no study to date has investigated the effect of feature-based attention on spatial sampling.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study based on literature review.

claim: When attention is endogenously cued, feature-based attention has been argued to influence the spatial resampling induced by spatial attention to optimize sampling of visual features for behavior.
source: Especially when attention is endogenously cued, feature-based attention has been argued to influence the spatial resampling induced by spatial attention to optimize sampling of visual features for behavior (Yeshurun and Carrasco, 1998; Yeshurun and Carrasco, 2000; Yeshurun et al., 2008; Barbot and Carrasco, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: When attending features that are processed by neurons with smaller receptive fields, a greater degree of spatial resampling is required to resolve the required featural resolution at the attended location.
source: Specifically, these authors suggested that when attending features that are processed by neurons with smaller receptive fields, a greater degree of spatial resampling is required to resolve the required featural resolution at the attended location.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior behavioral studies that the current study tests.

claim: Color is generally processed at a finer spatial scale compared to temporal frequency.
source: Specifically, color is generally processed at a finer spatial scale compared to temporal frequency.
evidence: This is established knowledge about visual processing supported by subsequent citations.

claim: Color compared to temporal frequency information is processed predominantly by the parvocellular rather than the magnocellular pathways, which pool differentially across visual space.
source: First, this is a result of color compared to temporal frequency information being processed predominantly by the parvocellular rather than the magnocellular pathways, which in turn pool differentially across visual space (Schiller and Malpeli, 1978; Hicks et al., 1983; Denison et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Temporal frequency and color are processed across different cortical areas (MT+ compared to hV4) that have differential spatial precision.
source: Second, temporal frequency and color are processed across different cortical areas (i.e. MT +compared to hV4; Liu and Wandell (2005); Brouwer and Heeger, 2009, Brouwer and Heeger, 2013; Winawer et al., 2010) that have differential spatial precision (Amano et al., 2009; Winawer et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Preference for color compared to temporal frequency is generally greater in the fovea compared to the periphery.
source: Third, preference for color compared to temporal frequency is generally greater in the fovea compared to the periphery (Curcio et al., 1990; Azzopardi et al., 1999; Brewer et al., 2005), where receptive fields are generally smaller (Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Attending color compared to temporal frequency at a particular location should lead to stronger spatial resampling.
source: The hypothesized relation between spatial scale of attended features and spatial resampling as proposed by the behavioral studies mentioned above thus implies that attending color compared to temporal frequency at a particular location should lead to stronger spatial resampling.
evidence: This is a hypothesis derived from prior research and tested in the current study.

claim: Attention can be directed to both temporal frequency and color feature domains.
source: It was previously shown that attention can be directed to both feature domains (Wolfe and Horowitz, 2004; Cass et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: pRF changes are stronger when attending the stimulus's color compared to temporal frequency content.
source: In brief, our results show that pRF changes are indeed stronger when attending the stimulus's color compared to temporal frequency content.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Feature-based attentional modulations occurred similarly throughout the visual system, regardless of an area's bottom-up feature preference.
source: These modulations occurred similarly throughout the visual system, regardless of an area's bottom-up feature preference.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Feature-based attentional modulations can be explained by changes in the precision of the attentional gain field.
source: We show that these feature-based attentional modulations can be explained by changes in the precision of the attentional gain field.
evidence: This is a finding based on modeling results.

claim: The degree of spatial resampling is dependent on the spatial scale at which attended features are processed.
source: Together, this confirms the idea that the degree of spatial resampling is dependent on the spatial scale at which attended features are processed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Five participants (two female, two authors, aged between 25 and 37) participated in the study.
source: Five participants (two female, two authors, aged between 25 and 37) participated in the study.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: All participants gave informed consent, and procedures were approved by the ethical review board of the University of Amsterdam (2016-BC-7145).
source: All gave informed consent, and procedures were approved by the ethical review board of the University of Amsterdam (2016-BC-7145), where scanning took place.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Behavioral difficulty was kept constant between conditions and across three levels of eccentricity using a Quest staircase procedure.
source: In addition, behavioral difficulty was kept constant between conditions and across three levels of eccentricity using a Quest staircase procedure.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: pRF shift magnitude increased up the visual hierarchy.
source: Visual inspection of these pRF position shifts shows both increasing shift magnitude up the visual hierarchy and shifts occurring mainly along the radial dimension (i.e. toward or away from the fovea; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding based on visual inspection of data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: pRF shifts occur mainly along the radial dimension (i.e. toward or away from the fovea).
source: Visual inspection of these pRF position shifts shows both increasing shift magnitude up the visual hierarchy and shifts occurring mainly along the radial dimension (i.e. toward or away from the fovea; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding based on visual inspection of data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Changes in pRF horizontal location consistently better describe the overall shifts than do changes of pRF vertical location in all ROIs except V1/2/3.
source: In line with the data of Sheremata and Silver (2015), we find that changes of pRF horizontal location consistently better describe the overall shifts than do changes of pRF vertical location in all ROIs except V1/2/3 (p's < 0.05, see Supplementary file 1 -Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of the data.

claim: pRF shifts are described even better by shifts in the radial dimension (i.e. changes in eccentricity) compared to shifts in the horizontal direction in all ROIs.
source: We also find that pRF shifts are described even better by shifts in the radial dimension (i.e. changes in eccentricity) compared to shifts in the horizontal direction in all ROIs (p's < 0.01, see Supplementary file 1 -Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The data correspond most to the radial shift hypothesis.
source: Figure 3D, right column, shows that the data (combined ROI) correspond most to the radial shift hypothesis.
evidence: This is a finding based on comparison of data to different hypotheses shown in Figure 3D.

claim: This pattern of results can only be explained by pRFs shifting in the radial direction.
source: This pattern of results can only be explained by pRFs shifting in the radial direction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical findings.

claim: Visual field coverage is non-uniform such that the horizontal meridian is overrepresented at both subcortical and cortical levels.
source: Visual field coverage is known to be non-uniform such that the horizontal meridian is overrepresented at both subcortical (Schneider et al., 2004) and cortical (Swisher et al., 2007; Silva et al., 2018) levels and was also clearly present in our data (Rayleigh tests for non-uniformity in ROIs separately, p's < 0.001, see Supplementary file 1 -Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and confirmed in the current data.

claim: Shifts that occur exclusively in the radial dimension appear as a dominance of horizontal compared to vertical shifts when averaging over the visual field.
source: This means that shifts that occur exclusively in the radial dimension appear as a dominance of horizontal compared to vertical shifts when averaging over the visual field.
evidence: This is an interpretation explaining the observed pattern of results.

claim: Overall, parafoveal pRFs shifted away from the fovea, while peripheral pRFs shifted toward the fovea.
source: The combined ROI shows that overall, parafoveal pRFs shifted away from the fovea, while peripheral pRFs shifted toward the fovea.
evidence: This is a finding based on analysis of data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Outward shifting parafoveal pRFs are found in all ROIs except V1 and V2.
source: These outward shifting parafoveal pRFs are found in all other ROIs except V1 and V2
evidence: This is a finding based on analysis of data across ROIs.

claim: Inward shifting peripheral pRFs are present in V1, V2 and V3.
source: whereas the inward shifting peripheral pRFs are also present in V1, V2 and V3 (see Supplementary file 1 -Tables 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a finding based on analysis of data across ROIs.

claim: Overall, parafoveal pRFs increased in size, while peripheral pRFs decreased in size.
source: Overall, parafoveal pRFs increased in size, while peripheral pRFs decreased in size.
evidence: This is a finding based on analysis of data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Expanding parafoveal pRFs were present in all ROIs except V2/3.
source: These expanding parafoveal pRFs were present in all ROIs except V2/3
evidence: This is a finding based on analysis of data across ROIs.

claim: Shrinking peripheral pRFs were found in all ROIs except V1, MT+ and IPS0.
source: whereas shrinking peripheral pRFs were found in all ROIs except V1, MT+ and IPS0 (see Supplementary file 1 -Tables 6 and 7).
evidence: This is a finding based on analysis of data across ROIs.

claim: The changes in pRF size and eccentricity were strongly correlated in all ROIs.
source: In fact, the changes in pRF size and eccentricity were strongly correlated in all ROIs (Figure 4C, Pearson R over 20 5-percentile bins between 0.74 and 0.99, p's < 0.001, see Supplementary file 1 -Table 8).
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Attention to the stimulus caused parafoveal pRFs to shift away from the fovea and increase in size, whereas peripheral pRFs shifted toward the fovea and decreased in size.
source: Together, these results show that attention to the stimulus caused parafoveal pRFs to shift away from the fovea and increase in size, whereas peripheral pRFs shifted toward the fovea and decreased in size.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the data analysis.

claim: Model predictions closely followed the data, thereby accurately reproducing radially shifting pRFs.
source: Figure 5A illustrates that model predictions closely followed the data, thereby accurately reproducing radially shifting pRFs.
evidence: This is a finding based on comparison of model predictions to data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The model was able to capture widely varying eccentricity change profiles across ROIs using very similar attentional gain field sizes.
source: Examining the predicted change in pRF eccentricity as a function of eccentricity (i.e. the dominant pRF shift direction; Figure 5B) showed that the model was able to capture widely varying eccentricity change profiles across ROIs using very similar attentional gain field sizes (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding based on modeling results shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: A common attentional influence can result in very different pRF shift patterns, which depend on differential spatial sampling properties across ROIs.
source: This shows that a common attentional influence can result in very different pRF shift patterns, which then depend on differential spatial sampling properties across ROIs (i.e. distribution of pRF sizes and positions).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: The attentional gain field model provides a parsimonious and powerful account for the variety of pRF shift patterns across ROIs.
source: In sum, these results show that the attentional gain field model provides a parsimonious and powerful account for the variety of pRF shift patterns across ROIs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Both sources of spatial attention pull the measured pRFs toward the fovea, albeit with differing relative magnitudes across eccentricity.
source: The left panels of each figure reveal the effects of attending fixation and the stimulus separately. This shows that both sources of spatial attention pull the measured pRFs toward the fovea, albeit with differing relative magnitudes across eccentricity.
evidence: This is a finding based on analysis of model components shown in Figures 5D-F.

claim: Existing multiplicative gain field models of attention can be extended to predict pRF shifts in situations where spatial attention shifts over time.
source: Together, these analyses show that existing multiplicative gain field models of attention can be extended to predict pRF shifts in situations where spatial attention shifts over time.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: The precision of the attentional gain field is similar across the visual hierarchy.
source: Additionally, it confirms, extends and quantifies earlier reports showing that the precision of the attentional gain field is similar across the visual hierarchy (Klein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results that confirms prior findings.

claim: While both tasks caused similar pRF changes, these effects were generally more pronounced when attending color.
source: Figure 6A shows how pRF eccentricity and size are differentially affected by attending color or temporal frequency within the stimulus for the combined ROI. This illustrates that while both tasks caused similar pRF changes, these effects were generally more pronounced when attending color.
evidence: This is a finding based on analysis of data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Positive values of feature AMI across eccentricity confirm stronger pRF modulations when attending color compared to TF.
source: Positive values of this feature AMI across eccentricity confirm stronger pRF modulations when attending color compared to TF.
evidence: This is a finding based on analysis of the feature AMI measure shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Attending changes in color compared to TF in the bar stimulus produced stronger spatial resampling in all ROIs.
source: Inspecting the average feature AMI across voxels within each ROI (Figure 6D) reveals that attending changes in color compared to TF in the bar stimulus produced stronger spatial resampling in all ROIs (p's < 0.01, see Supplementary file 1 -Table 9).
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The feature AMI was around 0.05 on average across ROIs, which corresponds to roughly 10% stronger pRF changes when attending color compared to temporal frequency.
source: Specifically, the feature AMI was around 0.05 on average across ROIs. As the feature AMI is a contrast measure where difference is divided by the sum, this corresponds to roughly 10% stronger pRF changes when attending color compared to temporal frequency.
evidence: This is a quantification of the effect size based on the data.

claim: In some ROIs (V3AB/IPS0), the FAMI reached values of 0.20, which corresponds roughly to 50% stronger pRF changes when attending color compared to temporal frequency.
source: In some ROIs (V3AB/IPS0, see Figure 6—figure supplement 1), the FAMI reached values of 0.20, which corresponds roughly to 50% stronger pRF changes when attending color compared to temporal frequency.
evidence: This is a quantification of the effect size in specific ROIs based on the data.

claim: Feature preference was negative on average in most ROIs, suggesting that the TF manipulation caused stronger response modulations compared to the color manipulation.
source: Note that feature preference was negative on average in most ROIs, suggesting that our TF manipulation (7 vs 0 Hz grayscale Gabors) caused stronger response modulations compared to our color manipulation (colored vs grayscale Gabors).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the feature preference data.

claim: Variations in feature preference across ROIs replicate known specializations of the visual system with high precision.
source: Although this induced an offset across the brain, variations in this measure across ROIs replicate known specializations of the visual system with high precision (Liu and Wandell, 2005; Brouwer and Heeger, 2009; Brouwer and Heeger, 2013)
evidence: This is a finding that the data replicate prior research.

claim: Areas MT+ and V1 show the strongest preference for TF compared to color, while areas V4 and VO show the strongest preference for color compared to TF.
source: while areas MT+ and V1 show the strongest preference for TF compared to color, areas V4 and VO show the strongest preference for color compared to TF.
evidence: This is a finding based on analysis of feature preference data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Regardless of large variations in feature preferences between MT+/V1 and VO/hV4, average feature AMI was nearly equal in these ROIs.
source: Importantly, regardless of these large variations in feature preferences between MT+/V1 and VO/hV4, average feature AMI was nearly equal in these ROIs.
evidence: This is a finding based on comparison of feature AMI across ROIs with different feature preferences.

claim: There was no correlation between feature preference and feature AMI across all ROIs.
source: In addition, there was no correlation between feature preference and feature AMI across all ROIs (R = 0.20, p = 0.608, N = 9, rho = 0.37, p = 0.332, N = 9).
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of the relationship between feature preference and feature AMI.

claim: The observed feature-based attentional modulations occur globally across the brain, and do not depend on bottom-up feature preference.
source: These results show that the observed feature-based attentional modulations occur globally across the brain, and do not depend on bottom-up feature preference.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of feature AMI and feature preference.

claim: Behavioral studies have suggested that the influence of spatial attention should be adjusted by feature-based attention to improve sampling of attended visual features.
source: Behavioral studies have suggested that the influence of spatial attention should be adjusted by feature-based attention to improve sampling of attended visual features (Yeshurun et al., 2008; Barbot and Carrasco, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Attending features processed by relatively smaller receptive fields requires a greater degree of spatial resampling.
source: Specifically, these authors suggested that attending features processed by relatively smaller receptive fields requires a greater degree of spatial resampling.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior behavioral studies.

claim: If color-preferring voxels are relatively small, this could explain the greater degree of resampling observed when attending color.
source: This implies that if color-preferring voxels are relatively small, this could explain the greater degree of resampling observed when attending color.
evidence: This is a hypothesis derived from prior research and the current findings.

claim: Color compared to temporal frequency information is predominantly processed by the parvocellular compared to the magnocellular pathway, where spatial sampling is generally more fine-grained.
source: This is indeed predicted by the fact that color compared to temporal frequency information is predominantly processed by the parvocellular compared to the magnocellular pathway, where spatial sampling is generally more fine-grained (Schiller and Malpeli, 1978; Hicks et al., 1983; Denison et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: pRF size is generally larger in area MT+ (preferring temporal frequency) compared to hV4 (preferring color).
source: In addition, pRF size varies on average between visual regions, such that pRF size is generally larger in area MT+ (preferring temporal frequency) compared to hV4 (preferring color).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pRF properties across visual areas.

claim: Both pRF size and color compared to TF preference are strongly eccentricity-dependent such that foveal voxels have relatively small pRFs and are relatively color-sensitive.
source: Finally, both pRF size (Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008) and color compared to TF preference (Curcio et al., 1990; Azzopardi et al., 1999; Brewer et al., 2005) are known to be strongly eccentricity-dependent such that foveal voxels have relatively small pRFs and are relatively color-sensitive.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The correlation between feature-preference and eccentricity is negative except in LO and VO.
source: We also clearly observe both effects in our data (see Figure 2B and Figure 7, correlation between feature-preference and eccentricity is negative except in LO and VO, see Supplementary file 1 - Table 10).
evidence: This is a finding based on analysis of the data shown in Figures 2B and 7.

claim: The greater amount of spatial resampling when attending color can be parsimoniously explained by color being sampled by relatively smaller pRFs.
source: In sum, the greater amount of spatial resampling when attending color can be parsimoniously explained by color being sampled by relatively smaller pRFs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of pRF properties and feature preferences.

claim: Smaller pRFs require a more precise attentional gain field to shift a given distance.
source: Smaller pRFs also require a more precise attentional gain field to shift a given distance (a property of the multiplication of Gaussians).
evidence: This is a mathematical property of Gaussian multiplication.

claim: Attentional gain fields should be more precise when attending color compared to temporal frequency.
source: Combining this with our observation that pRFs experience greater shifts when attending color, we predict that attentional gain fields should be more precise in this condition.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the mathematical properties and observed data.

claim: Fitted stimulus attentional gain field sizes were smaller in the Attend Color compared to the Attend TF fit procedure in the combined ROI.
source: This analysis returned smaller fitted stimulus attentional gain field sizes in the Attend Color compared to the Attend TF fit procedure (Figure 8) both in the combined ROI (0.094 dva smaller over subjects when attending color, t(4) = 9.021, p = 0.001, Cohen's d = 4.511)
evidence: This is a finding based on modeling results shown in Figure 8.

claim: Fitted stimulus attentional gain field sizes were smaller in the Attend Color compared to the Attend TF fit procedure across ROIs.
source: and across ROIs (median over ROIs on average 0.061 dva smaller over subjects when attending color, t(4) = 4.243, p = 0.013, Cohen's d = 2.121).
evidence: This is a finding based on modeling results across ROIs.

claim: The estimated fixation attentional gain field was not different between Attend Color and Attend TF procedures.
source: As the Attend Fixation data were used as input in both modeling procedures, we verified that the estimated fixation attentional gain field was not different between procedures (p's of. 693 and. 224 and Cohen's d of −0.213 and −0.719 for across ROIs and combined ROI, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical comparison of model parameters.

claim: The stronger influence of spatial attention when attending color is realized by a more precise attentional gain field located at the stimulus.
source: These analyses show that the stronger influence of spatial attention when attending color is realized by a more precise attentional gain field located at the stimulus.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: The attentional system adjusts its influence in accordance with the spatial sampling characteristics of units that prefer the attended feature.
source: In sum, our results suggest that (1) the attentional system adjusts its influence in accordance with the spatial sampling characteristics of units that prefer the attended feature
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: The attentional system adjusts its influence equally across visual regions regardless of their bottom-up feature preference.
source: and (2) that it does this equally across visual regions regardless of their bottom-up feature preference.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: Although spatial attention resulted in somewhat different patterns of pRF shifts between subjects, these individual differences were well captured by the attentional gain field model.
source: This showed that although spatial attention resulted in somewhat different patterns of pRF shifts between subjects, these individual differences were well captured by the attentional gain field model.
evidence: This is a finding from the across-subject consistency analysis.

claim: Individual differences in pRF changes are likely the result of known individual differences in pRF parameter distributions.
source: This suggests that individual differences in pRF changes are likely the result of the known individual differences in pRF parameter distributions (e.g. eccentricity-size relations [Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and see Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008]).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the across-subject consistency analysis.

claim: When predicting gaze position, the evidence was in favor of the null hypothesis with a Bayes Factor of 18620.
source: We found that when predicting gaze position, the evidence was in favor of the null hypothesis with a Bayes Factor (BF) of 18620.
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian analysis of eye tracking data.

claim: When predicting gaze variability, evidence was found against the null hypothesis with a BF of 5.980.
source: When predicting gaze variability, however, we found evidence against the null hypothesis with a BF of 5.980.
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian analysis of eye tracking data.

claim: Bar position influenced gaze variability but did not do so differently between attention conditions.
source: More importantly, the analyses also showed that although bar position influenced gaze variability (BF of 547.193), it did not do so differently between attention conditions (BF of 0.017).
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian analysis of eye tracking data.

claim: The Quest procedure successfully equated performance across attention conditions and eccentricity levels.
source: To verify whether the Quest procedure successfully equated performance, we used a similar Bayesian approach, testing whether a model including attention condition (three levels) and stimulus eccentricity (three levels) influenced behavioral performance (Figure 9A). This returned evidence for the null hypothesis with a BF of 6.25.
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian analysis of behavioral performance data.

claim: Differences in pRF parameters between conditions cannot be explained by either fixation accuracy or behavioral difficulty.
source: Together, these results show that differences in pRF parameters between conditions cannot be explained by either fixation accuracy or behavioral difficulty.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of eye tracking and behavioral data.

claim: Directing covert spatial attention toward a moving bar stimulus altered the eccentricity and size of pRFs in concert.
source: We found that directing covert spatial attention toward a moving bar stimulus altered the eccentricity and size of pRFs in concert.
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings in the Discussion.

claim: Changes in spatial sampling were parsimoniously explained by an attentional gain field model.
source: These changes in spatial sampling were parsimoniously explained by an attentional gain field model.
evidence: This is a summary of modeling findings in the Discussion.

claim: Attending color changes within the stimulus induced stronger pRF changes compared to attending temporal frequency changes.
source: Attending color changes within this stimulus induced stronger pRF changes compared to attending temporal frequency changes.
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings in the Discussion.

claim: Feature-based attentional modulations occurred globally throughout the brain, irrespective of a visual region's average feature preference.
source: These feature-based attentional modulations occurred globally throughout the brain, irrespective of a visual region's average feature preference.
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings in the Discussion.

claim: The greater degree of spatial resampling when attending color is related to smaller pRF sizes in relatively color preferring voxels.
source: We suggest that the greater degree of spatial resampling when attending color is related to smaller pRF sizes in relatively color preferring voxels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of pRF properties and feature preferences.

claim: The greater degree of spatial resampling when attending color is caused by a more precise attentional gain field on the stimulus.
source: In addition, we showed that the greater degree of spatial resampling when attending color is caused by a more precise attentional gain field on the stimulus.
evidence: This is a summary of modeling findings in the Discussion.

claim: The greater degree of spatial resampling when attending color compared to temporal frequency could be explained by color being sampled at a finer spatial scale.
source: This means that the greater degree of spatial resampling when attending color compared to temporal frequency could be explained by color being sampled at a finer spatial scale.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the Discussion.

claim: The results should generalize to any other comparison of attended visual features as long as these features differ in their spatial scale.
source: We therefore predict that our results should generalize to any other comparison of attended visual features as long as these features differ in their spatial scale.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the current findings.

claim: Feature-based attention modulates the effects of spatial attention on spatial resampling.
source: We add to this (1) that feature-based attention modulates the effects of spatial attention on spatial resampling
evidence: This is a summary of the study's contribution to the literature.

claim: Interactions between spatial and feature-based attention occur globally throughout the brain, manifesting themselves in even the earliest cortical visual regions.
source: and (2) that these interactions occur globally throughout the brain, manifesting themselves in even the earliest cortical visual regions.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's contribution to the literature.

claim: Measuring spatial sampling at the level of voxels does not allow determination of whether observed changes are the result of changes in spatial sampling of individual neurons or differential weighting of subpopulations of neurons within a voxel.
source: However, it is important to note that measuring spatial sampling at the level of voxels does not allow us to determine whether observed changes in spatial sampling are the result of changes in spatial sampling of individual neurons, or rather the result of differential weighting of subpopulations of neurons within a voxel.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged in the Discussion.

claim: Spatial attention influences spatial sampling of individual neurons.
source: Nevertheless, it has been shown that spatial attention does influence spatial sampling of individual neurons (Connor et al., 1997; Womelsdorf et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The global pattern of pRF shifts could be caused by an object-based attentional transfer mechanism.
source: This could mean that the global pattern of pRF shifts we observed is caused by such an object-based attentional transfer mechanism.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The global nature of spatial resampling supports a temporally dynamic but spatially consistent adaptation of visual space.
source: Instead, the global nature of spatial resampling we observe supports a temporally dynamic but spatially consistent adaptation of visual space.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Signals of spatial selection are thought to originate from a network of frontal and parietal areas.
source: Signals of spatial selection are thought to originate from a network of frontal and parietal areas, identified using fMRI (Shulman et al., 2002; Silver et al., 2005; Jerde et al., 2012; Sprague and Serences, 2013; Szczepanski et al., 2013; Kay and Yeatman, 2017; Mackey et al., 2017) and electrophysiology (Moore and Armstrong, 2003; Gregoriou et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The ventral prearcuate gyrus may play a central role for conjoined spatial and feature-based attentional modulations.
source: A recent study suggested a central role for the ventral prearcuate gyrus for conjoined spatial and feature-based attentional modulations (Bichot et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The inferior frontal junction (IFJ) is a possible candidate for controlling the interactions between feature-based and spatial attention.
source: Correspondingly, signals of feature selection in humans have been localized to a likely human homologue of this area, the inferior frontal junction (IFJ; Zanto et al., 2010; Baldauf and Desimone, 2014). This region is therefore a possible candidate for controlling the interactions between feature-based and spatial attention.
evidence: This is a speculation based on prior research.

claim: The average changes in pRF size and eccentricity for each visual region are largely consistent with previous studies in which attention was devoted to a peripheral stimulus versus fixation.
source: The average changes in pRF size and eccentricity for each visual region in our data are largely consistent with previous studies in which attention was devoted to a peripheral stimulus versus fixation (Kay et al., 2015; Sheremata and Silver, 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to prior research.

claim: Attending the stimulus compared to fixation caused pRFs to shift radially.
source: First, we show that attending the stimulus compared to fixation caused pRFs to shift radially.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding.

claim: The overrepresentation of the horizontal meridian made radially shifting pRFs appear as predominantly horizontal changes.
source: Although a previous study reported a dominant horizontal shift direction (Sheremata and Silver, 2015), we suggest that the overrepresentation of the horizontal meridian (Schneider et al., 2004; Swisher et al., 2007) made radially shifting pRFs appear as predominantly horizontal changes.
evidence: This is an interpretation that reconciles the current findings with prior research.

claim: Parafoveal pRFs shifted toward the periphery and increased in size, whereas peripheral pRFs shifted toward the fovea and decreased in size.
source: Second, we report closely coupled pRF eccentricity and size changes that were dependent on pRF eccentricity. Specifically, we found that parafoveal pRFs shifted toward the periphery and increased in size, whereas peripheral pRFs shifted toward the fovea and decreased in size.
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings.

claim: This finding supports the resolution hypothesis of attention.
source: This finding supports the resolution hypothesis of attention (Anton-Erxleben and Carrasco, 2013), which posits that spatial attention acts to reduce resolution differences between the fovea and periphery.
evidence: This is an interpretation that relates the findings to a theoretical framework.

claim: The functional implication of pRF size changes was recently questioned, as stimulus encoding fidelity was shown to be unaffected by pRF size changes.
source: We note that the functional implication of pRF size changes was recently questioned, as stimulus encoding fidelity was shown to be unaffected by pRF size changes (Vo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The attentional gain field model extends to situations in which attention is dynamically deployed over space and time during the mapping of the pRF.
source: Second, it extends the utility of such attentional gain field models to situations in which attention is dynamically deployed over space and time during the mapping of the pRF (Kay et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary of the study's contribution to modeling approaches.

claim: The best-fitting model implemented comparable attentional gain field sizes across visual regions.
source: In agreement with earlier reports (Klein et al., 2014; Puckett and DeYoe, 2015), we found that the best-fitting model implemented comparable attentional gain field sizes across visual regions.
evidence: This is a finding that confirms prior research.

claim: Differences in pRF shift patterns between different visual regions depended primarily on differences in visual sampling rather than on differing attentional influences.
source: We conclude that differences in pRF shift patterns between different visual regions depended primarily on differences in visual sampling (i.e. differences in pRF center and size distributions) rather than on differing attentional influences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: The model did not capture the observed decreases in pRF eccentricity of the most foveal pRFs in V1.
source: Despite the broad correspondence between model fits and data, the model did not capture the observed decreases in pRF eccentricity of the most foveal pRFs in V1.
evidence: This is a limitation of the model noted in the Discussion.

claim: In early visual areas, spatial attention shifted pRFs away from the attended location, but toward the attended location in higher visual areas.
source: Two recent studies showed that in early visual areas, spatial attention shifted pRFs away from the attended location, but toward the attended location in higher visual areas (de Haas et al., 2014; Vo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In early visual regions, both the pRF and the attentional gain field are composed of a suppressive surround in addition to their positive peak.
source: Other studies showed that in precisely these visual regions, both the pRF and the attentional gain field are composed of a suppressive surround in addition to their positive peak (Zuiderbaan et al., 2012; Puckett and DeYoe, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Gain fields have been shown to influence visual processing at the motor stage.
source: As a more general aside, gain fields have been shown to influence visual processing at the motor stage (Van Opstal et al., 1995; Snyder et al., 1998; Trotter and Celebrini, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The results establish the close link between attentional and motor processes.
source: Thus, our results further establish the close link between attentional and motor processes (Rizzolatti et al., 1987; Corbetta et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an interpretation that relates the findings to prior research.

claim: The global nature of these modulations highlights the flexibility of the brain's encoding of sensory information to meet task demands.
source: The global nature of these modulations highlights the flexibility of the brain's encoding of sensory information to meet task demands (Rosenholtz, 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in a broader context.
